rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-2.3 and 3 - continuous eddy-covariance measurements of carbon and water fluxes at the Daman seed-maize site from 2012 to 2018, with flood irrigation before 2017 and drip irrigation under film mulch from 2017. Q2: Section 3.2, Table 2 and Figure 7 - annual ET fell from about 733 to 640 kg H2O m-2 (about -13%) and ecosystem/canopy WUE rose by 9.3-13.6% and 10.5-11.0% after the switch from flood to drip irrigation in maize; Abstract and Conclusions state drip is an effective method to reduce irrigation water use and raise WUE. Q4: Table 2, Figures 4-6 and Section 4.2 - the study measures soil moisture at 4, 40 and 160 cm (decreases of 27-32% shallow and 36-42% deep under drip, reduced deep percolation) and partitions ET into soil evaporation and transpiration (E decreased about 20%, more than T), i.e. the intermediate variables through which drip reduces water use and raises WUE.
rows.notes: Single flux-tower footprint on one maize field, one site, one crop; before/after comparison across years rather than paired treatments, so interannual climate variation is confounded with the irrigation change (study does not state this as a limitation). The drip-vs-flood effect rests on one method (EC fluxes plus PM-Leuning model partitioning); lysimeter and isotope data were only used to validate the model in 2012 under flood irrigation, so no independent second method on the drip effect. The 9-14% range reflects two alternative data subsets (2018 only vs 2017-2018 mean) rather than a dispersion statistic; the <U+00B1>0.17 and <U+00B1>0.21 values are for mean WUE over the whole period, not for the drip effect. Table 2 note acknowledges differing drip intensity/frequency between 2017 and 2018 but this is not framed as a limitation of the result. Film mulch was used in both periods, so the comparison isolates drip vs flood.

notes: Full text available; some figure captions and paragraphs are duplicated by PDF extraction but content is complete.
